meta.description: Demonstration dataset covering the 13 West Africa Sustainable Ocean Programme (WASOP) countries and 9 additional African countries. It combines detailed Guinea-Bissau research (Bijagós Archipelago, Cacheu region, Cantanhez), researched challenges and potential activities for one area in each other WASOP country, and a partial, source-checked protected-area inventory for all 22 countries: nationally designated areas from national authorities and legal texts, Ramsar sites, World Heritage properties and biosphere reserves. No country inventory has been verified as exhaustive. Every factual statement cites a publicly accessible source that was checked on the access date shown. Potential regenerative activities are presented as interpretations or hypotheses, never as validated businesses.

inventory.summary: National parks, hunting zones and MPAs are PA categories under the wildlife regime (Décret 2011-394); Pendjari NP is under delegated management (6NR). The NBSAP Tableau 1 (DGFRN 2013) gives official counts by category (2 national parks, 4 zones cynégétiques, 46 forêts classées, 6 périmètres de reboisement) but no names; two MPAs were created in 2022. cenagref.net was not used (reported hijacked). Comparison: the sources reviewed list 9 nationally designated or proposed areas; 3 are catalogued here, and 6 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

inventory.summary: The legal inventory is the annex 'Rede Nacional Inicial de Áreas Protegidas' of Decreto-Lei n.º 3/2003 of 24 February 2003 (regime jurídico dos espaços naturais; amended by Decreto-Lei n.º 44/2006), which declares 47 areas by island in six categories (Parque Nacional, Parque Natural, Reserva Natural, Monumento Natural, Paisagem Protegida, Sítio de Interesse Científico). Individual areas are subsequently delimited by Decreto-Regulamentar and given management plans by Resolução; some categories and limits have changed since 2003 (e.g. Barreiro e Figueira now a Paisagem Protegida). All 47 annex entries are recorded below with the 2003 category; later instruments verified in FAOLEX are added to legalStatus. Later additions to the network (if any) were not systematically searched. The 2003 annex is an official list but only as a scanned gazette page (not machine-readable). Comparison: the sources reviewed list 47 nationally designated or proposed areas; 20 are catalogued here (1 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 27 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

inventory.summary: Wildlife protected areas are designated under the Biodiversity/Wildlife Act 2003 and managed by the Department of Parks and Wildlife Management (DPWM); forest reserves/parks are under the Department of Forestry. The best official list found is Table 1 'Protected Areas of the Gambia' in the revised NBSAP (March 2015), giving 22 entries (7 established parks/reserves, 1 proposed national park, 1 community wildlife reserve and 13 community conservation areas then 'in process'). The 6th national report (2019) repeats the count of 22 wildlife protected areas (8 reserves/national parks + 14 community-based conservation areas) without names. No DPWM-published list was used (dpwm.gov.gm reported hijacked/dead). Comparison: the sources reviewed list 24 nationally designated or proposed areas; 7 are catalogued here (2 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 17 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 3 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

The status of the 13 community conservation areas listed 'in process' in 2015 is inferred, not confirmed by name, from NR6's statement that 13 new community protected areas were established.

inventory.summary: No published official list of Guinea's protected areas was found. Guinea's PoWPA document (CBD) says the national protected-area network was 'validated' in 2010 with 53 identified protected areas, many without validated creation acts, but gives no list. Management lies with the Office Guinéen des Parcs Nationaux et Réserves de Faune (OGPNRF) and the forestry administration; Mount Nimba is managed by CEGENS. The most detailed descriptive source is the 2008 IUCN/PAPACO management-effectiveness evaluation of 12 areas (hosted on Guinea's national CBD clearing-house), which itself warns that the legal status of most areas has not been updated since independence. Records below combine that evaluation with Guinea's 6th (2018) and 7th (2026) CBD reports and the Haut Niger creation decree; legal status is uncertain for several sites. Ramsar sites are handled separately. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 14 nationally designated or proposed areas; 9 are catalogued here (3 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 5 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 15 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

inventory.summary: The Sistema Nacional de Áreas Protegidas (SNAP) is managed by the Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP) under the Lei-Quadro das Áreas Protegidas (Decreto-Lei 5-A/2011, replacing Decreto-Lei 3/97). IBAP's website lists the protected areas and publishes the creation decrees (scanned Boletim Oficial pages), which were checked for the 2000, 2005, 2011 and 2017 decrees. The 6th CBD report (2019) states the SNAP covers 26.3% of the territory (~750,000 ha) with 8 protected areas plus 3 ecological corridors created by Decrees 11–15/2017. The list appears complete for state protected areas; community forests (104) are not enumerated. Note: the IBAP website (ibapgbissau.org) also carries unrelated spam blog posts, suggesting partial compromise; facts were cross-checked against the decree scans and NR6. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 11 nationally designated or proposed areas; 6 are catalogued here (5 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 5 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

inventory.summary: No standalone official register was found. The most explicit official statement is Mauritania's 6th CBD national report (2019, section 7.2 'Situation des aires protégées'), which lists two national parks (Banc d'Arguin, Diawling), a recently created third park (Awleigatt), the Cap Blanc satellite reserve and the (unclassified) Chat Tboul reserve, plus several areas under study. The two main parks are public administrative establishments with their own laws/decrees and official websites (pnba.mr, pnd.mr); a Direction des aires protégées et du littoral (DAPL) exists within the environment ministry. The 'Zones protégées' page of the national CBD clearing-house (mr.chm-cbd.net) reproduces outdated WCMC-derived entries and was not used. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 7 nationally designated or proposed areas; 4 are catalogued here (3 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 3 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

inventory.summary: Federal national parks are managed by the Nigeria National Park Service (NPS) under the National Park Service Act (Cap N65 LFN 2004, amended 2006), whose s.50 lists the seven pre-existing parks. Ten additional parks were declared by the National Park (Declaration) Order 2022 (National Assembly concurrence March 2023; NPS says gazetted) and are being handed over by the states in batches (Hadejia Wetlands, Oba Hills and Marhai in 2024; Kampe in Feb 2025), giving 17 national parks per NPS. Game reserves and forest reserves are state-managed; no official machine-readable or enumerable national list of them was found. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 18 nationally designated or proposed areas; 11 are catalogued here, and 7 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 16 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

inventory.summary: No single consolidated, current official list was found online. Protected areas are split between the Direction des Parcs Nationaux (DPN: national parks, special/fauna reserves), the Direction des Aires Marines Communautaires Protégées (DAMCP, created by decree 2012-543: marine protected areas and coastal community reserves) and the forestry service DEFCCS (213 forêts classées, sylvopastoral reserves, hunting zones). The best official lists found are: the DPN's PoWPA document (table of 16 DPN-administered areas, c. 2011), the 2013 National MPA Strategy (14 coastal areas), Senegal's 2018 AEWA national-report annex (22 sites incl. later AMPs), and individual creation decrees (2004, 2014, 2020, 2023). Lists are dated and partial; the DPN and DAMCP websites were not used (reported hijacked/dead). Comparison: the sources reviewed list 28 nationally designated or proposed areas; 19 are catalogued here (9 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 9 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 9 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

NPAA's website has a 'List of National Protected Areas' page, but it was empty when fetched (Oct 2026) and the site contains template placeholder content. The best official descriptions are the NBSAP 2017–2026 (protected-area categories under the Wildlife Conservation Act 1972, gazetted national parks, Table 9 of major forest-estate components, Table 2 of estuarine MPAs) and the 6th CBD national report (2020). inventory.summary: The Ministère de l'Environnement et des Ressources Forestières (MERF) is responsible for PAs. Of 83 legally classified PAs (to 1990), a requalification programme (since 1999; décret 2003-237/PR) retained 10-14 priority PAs covering ~578,000 ha. No consolidated official list with legal acts exists in sources seen; records combine the government PoWPA table, NBSAP 2014, 6NR (2018) and the UICN 2008 RAPPAM. A new law on creation and management of PAs was adopted by the National Assembly in August 2026 (promulgation not verified). Comparison: the sources reviewed list 14 nationally designated or proposed areas; 6 are catalogued here (1 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 8 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: The national conservation-area network is managed by INBAC (Instituto Nacional da Biodiversidade e Áreas de Conservação, under the ministry responsible for the environment, currently the Ministério da Cultura, Turismo e Ambiente per INBAC park pages). INBAC's website lists 14 areas — 9 national parks, 1 regional natural park (Chimalavera) and 4 reserves — with creating instruments and areas on each page; this matches the counts in the 2019-2025 NBSAP and INBAC's November 2023 status report (156,909.9 km2, 12.58% of the territory). No machine-readable register exists. The legal framework is Lei 8/20 (Áreas de Conservação Ambiental), amended by Lei 12/21. Four further areas, including the first marine conservation area (Baía dos Tigres), are being created but no creating instrument was found. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 18 nationally designated or proposed areas; 10 are catalogued here, and 8 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 1 Ramsar site for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

officialCounts.category: conservation areas (9 national parks, 1 natural park, 4 reserves)

gaps: INBAC pages contain copy-paste errors (Mupa page cites 'Reserva natural integral de Bicuar'; Bicuar page says the 1964 diploma created a 'Reserva parcial'; Cameia's Portaria number and date are blank) — legal histories should be checked against the original Boletim Oficial texts, which were not available online.
Luengue-Luiana area conflicts: 22,610 km2 in Lei 38/11 vs 45,816/45,818 km2 in INBAC documents (possibly reflecting later boundary changes not found).
INBAC's conservation-areas document (ago-inbac-acs) highlights an extension of Iona's limits into the marine environment; no instrument confirming a marine extension was found.

Status of the four areas 'em criação' (Cumbira, Morro do Moco, Serra do Pingano, Baía dos Tigres) after November 2023 could not be confirmed from a Diário da República text; as of the October 2026 State of the Nation report Baía dos Tigres was still being advanced.
Lei 8/20 was only available as a scanned PDF (checked by OCR); it defines categories but does not itself list the existing areas.
No official coordinates were used; points depend on Wikidata matches. Chimalavera and Ilhéu dos Pássaros had no matching Wikidata item in a keyword search (Wikidata was rate-limited during this run).

Not enumerated: coutadas (public and private hunting areas) — Hunting concessions, not conservation areas under Lei 8/20; no official current list found (Lei 38/11 names Longa-Mavinga, Luengue, Luiana and Mucusso coutadas partly absorbed into Luengue-Luiana).
Not enumerated: forest reserves (reservas florestais) — No official list found online.
8 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: No public protected-area register from the Department of Wildlife and National Parks (DWNP) was found online (DWNP has no standalone website; the Botswana Tourism site returned errors). The authoritative list is statutory: the Wildlife Conservation and National Parks Act (Cap. 38:01) declares national parks (First Schedule), game reserves and sanctuaries (Second Schedule), wildlife management areas (Third Schedule) and controlled hunting areas (Fourth Schedule). The freely available consolidated text (FAOLEX) runs to 2007; the Sua Pan Flamingo Sanctuary (S.I. 38 of 2010) was added from its own order. Forest reserves come from the Forest (Declaration of Forest Reserves) Order. The current (2023-2024 amended) consolidated Act is behind a paywall, so later changes may be missing. Category totals from the 5th CBD report (2015, Table 5): national parks 44,390 km2 (7%); game reserves 59,590 + 408 km2 (10%); legislated WMAs 72,090 km2 (23%) plus 65,780 km2 not legislated; forest reserves 4,095.4 km2 (1%). DWNP's PoWPA submission: 'About 40% of the Botswana’s land area has been devoted to protected areas, with 17% being national parks and game reserves'. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 29 nationally designated or proposed areas; 10 are catalogued here, and 19 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 1 Ramsar site for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.
gaps: The freely available consolidated Wildlife Conservation and National Parks Act (FAOLEX) is current only to S.I. 80 of 2007; amendments by Act 15 of 2023 and S.I.s of 2023-2024 could not be read (paywalled), so any newer parks, reserves or WMAs are missing.
Establishment years for national parks and game reserves (pre-1992 declarations under the National Parks Act and Fauna Conservation Act) were not found in an official source and are left null.
Per-area sizes are not given in the Act or the 5th CBD report (which only gives category totals), so areaKm2 is null except where stated.

Areas often described as protected (Khama Rhino Sanctuary, Mokolodi Nature Reserve, Nata Bird Sanctuary, Mashatu, Okavango Delta as a whole) do not appear in the Act's schedules; they are community, private or international designations and were not added.
Current status of the forest reserves after the partial degazetting noted in the 5th CBD report (2015) was not verified.

No official coordinates were used; points depend on Wikidata matches. Gemsbok National Park has no QID because Wikidata only has the binational Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park (Q859385); sanctuaries, WMAs and most forest reserves had no matching item (Wikidata was rate-limited, so only a keyword search was run).

Not enumerated: controlled hunting areas (Fourth Schedule) (about 80) — Hunting/land-use zoning units (NG/, CH/, GH/ etc.), not protected areas; 80 numbered entries counted in the 2007 consolidated Fourth Schedule.
Not enumerated: private game reserves (Declaration of Private Game Reserve(s) Orders) — Declared farm by farm under orders amended many times (1968-2008); full current list not freely available.
Not enumerated: non-legislated (proposed) wildlife management areas — 5th CBD report: Kgalagadi District WMAs have land board approval but were not gazetted (65,780 km2 'not legislated').
19 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: The Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency (EEAA, Nature Conservation Sector) maintains the official list of natural protectorates declared by Prime Ministerial decree under Law No. 102 of 1983. Its July 2026 list (English and Arabic PDFs) enumerates all 31 protectorates with declaration year, area, governorate, management type and declaring/amending decrees; this matches the count of 31 (up to 2025) stated on the EEAA protectorates page. The list appears complete for nationally declared protectorates. It is a PDF table, not a dataset, and gives no coordinates or boundaries. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 31 nationally designated or proposed areas; 20 are catalogued here (3 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 11 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.
gaps: No official coordinates or boundaries were found; the EEAA protectorates map (https://www.eeaa.gov.eg/Uploads/Topics/Files/20230308115635941.pdf, 2023) is image-only, so coordinates are left null.

Marine/coastal flags rely on EEAA's short descriptions; protectorates whose description does not mention marine or coastal waters (e.g. Zaranik/Bardawil, Ashtum El-Gamil, Burullus, Taba, Salloum Gulf, Al-Omayed) are left null rather than guessed.

The boundaries of the 2025 Great Fringing Reefs protectorate (Decree 4419/2025), and how it overlaps the existing Red Sea protectorates, were not verified from an official text; the decree itself was not obtained.
The EEAA page notes that protectorate pages are being updated; the English 'Regulations' PDF on the page is image-only and was not used.
Arabic local names come from a PDF whose text extraction breaks lam-alef ligatures; they were corrected by hand and should be spot-checked.
Ramsar, World Heritage and Biosphere overlaps are mentioned only where EEAA text or well-known coincidence supports them; the coordinator should confirm them from Ramsar/UNESCO.

Wikidata QIDs were checked one by one with Special:EntityData (label incl. Arabic, P17=Egypt, P31). No item was found for Nile River Islands, Gebel Kamil Meteorite or Great Fringing Reefs. The Dababiya, Salloum and Bahariya items are bare protected-area items without coordinates. Elba also has a second, bare item (Q117258352) besides the one used (Q47069184). Omayed's item is typed as a biosphere reserve but carries the protectorate's Arabic name.
11 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: No consolidated official list was retrievable online: the ANPN (Agence Nationale des Parcs Nationaux) website did not resolve/respond. The inventory here is assembled from the founding legal texts: the 13 decrees of 30 August 2002 classifying the national parks (FAOLEX/LEAP; governed since by Loi 003/2007) and Décret 00161/PR of 31 May 2017, which creates 9 marine parks and 11 aquatic reserves with areas and boundaries. Counts are confirmed by Gabon's 6th national report to the CBD (2019). Other protected areas (presidential reserve, arboreta, hunting domains, proposed sites) come from the 2012 PoWPA action plan and the 2019 national report and are dated or partly verified. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 46 nationally designated or proposed areas; 18 are catalogued here (5 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 28 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 8 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.
gaps: The ANPN website (parcsgabon.ga / anpn.ga) could not be reached (DNS failure/timeout), so no current official ANPN list was checked; possible changes after 2019 (new parks, boundary changes, the extension of Akanda/Pongara buffer zones or the May 2026 draft partial declassification of Arboretum Raponda Walker reported in the press) are not verified.

National park areas are the classification-decree figures from 2002 (FAOLEX abstracts or scanned decrees). Later boundary changes, if any, are not reflected. The LEAP abstract for decree 615 (Minkébé) is wrong (it repeats Moukalaba-Doudou), so the Minkébé area comes from the scanned decree.

Gabon's 6th national report swaps the marine totals (aquatic reserves 173,100 ha; marine parks 5,102,800 ha); Decree 161/2017 gives marine parks 1,731 km² and aquatic reserves 51,028 km², and the decree figures are used here.
Decree 161/2017 gives boundary coordinates for each marine park and aquatic reserve. They were not converted to points, so coordinates are left null.

The status of hunting domains (domaines de chasse) and of Wonga-Wongué rests on the 2012 PoWPA table only. Their creating acts were not found, and several probably overlap or were absorbed by the 2002 national parks.
Marine flags for Mayumba and Moukalaba-Doudou national parks are left null because the fetched texts do not describe them as marine or coastal.
Ramsar, World Heritage (Lopé, 2015) and biosphere (Ipassa-Makokou) overlaps are noted only as stated in the 6th national report.

Wikidata QIDs were checked with Special:EntityData (label, P17=Gabon, P31). The 20 marine-network items and most hunting-domain items have no coordinates on Wikidata. No QID was assigned to Lékédi (the Wikidata 'parc de la Lékédi' may not be the same unit), Arboretum de Sibang, Iboudji or Evaro. The Raponda Walker record is linked to 'Mondah Forest' (Q6898591).
Not enumerated: classified forests (forêts classées) and other forest reserves — No official list found; only Sibang and Mondah appear in the 2012 PoWPA table.
Not enumerated: conservation series (séries de conservation) in managed forest concessions — Mentioned in the 6th national report as additional conservation areas, but not listed.
28 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: ANAC (Administração Nacional das Áreas de Conservação) administers the national system of conservation areas and its website lists 10 national parks, 2 national reserves and 1 special reserve (plus transfrontier areas), but its 'sobre' text is out of date ('7 Parques e 7 Reservas Nacionais') and it does not list environmental protection areas, partial reserves or municipal parks. Creation instruments are decrees published in the Boletim da República (several available on FAOLEX). Hunting areas (20 coutadas oficiais, 9 blocos de caça, 13 community programmes, 31 fazendas do bravio) are stated by ANAC without a published list. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 16 nationally designated or proposed areas; 11 are catalogued here, and 5 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 2 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

officialCounts.category: national parks and national reserves (ANAC 'sobre', dated)

gaps: The 2020 recategorisation decrees (Gilé and Chimanimani to national parks; Niassa to special reserve) were not located; the status rests on ANAC's current list plus a dated news report (and, for Chimanimani, a 2022 Boletim despacho naming the national park).
Creation instruments and dates for Gorongosa, Banhine, Zinave, Marromeu, Pomene and Niassa were not verified from legal texts (only ANAC's narrative years).
ANAC still lists Marromeu and Pomene as 'Reserva Nacional' although that category was reportedly abolished by Lei 5/2017; their current legal category is unclear.
Areas: only Bazaruto (ANAC), Quirimbas (ANAC, approximate) and the Primeiras e Segundas APA (decree) have documented areas; the CBD 5NR table contains garbled hectare figures.

Lake Niassa Partial Reserve and the Primeiras e Segundas APA are not on ANAC's conservation-areas page; Ponta do Ouro Partial Marine Reserve and Maputo Special Reserve were extinguished in 2021 and merged into Maputo National Park, so they are not recorded separately.
Transfrontier conservation areas (Grande Limpopo, Lubombo, Niassa-Selous, ZIMOZA) are treaty frameworks over national areas, not separate national designations, and are not recorded.
No official coordinates were found (decrees contain boundary coordinates but no single reference point).

Wikidata QIDs were matched (search + entity check of label, P17 country and P31 type) only for national parks and selected major reserves; the Wikidata API was heavily rate-limited (HTTP 429) during this run, so other areas were not attempted or the lookup failed. A null QID does not mean no item exists.

Not enumerated: coutadas oficiais (official hunting areas) (about 20) — Hunting areas; ANAC states the count but publishes no list. Under Lei 16/2014 they are sustainable-use conservation areas, but per the brief they are not recorded without an official list.
Not enumerated: fazendas do bravio (game farms) (about 31) — Private/commercial hunting areas; no official list found.

Not enumerated: community conservation areas / community hunting programmes (e.g. Tchuma Tchato, Chipanje Chetu) (about 13) — ANAC mentions 13 community programmes; no list or legal designations found.

Not enumerated: forest reserves, sanctuaries and municipal ecological parks — No official consolidated list found (e.g. Santuário Bravio de Vilanculos, Cabo de São Sebastião, Inhaca reserves were seen only in non-official sources).
5 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: State protected areas are managed by the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism (MEFT); its website lists 20 state protected areas (national parks, game parks, recreation resorts, Cape Cross Seal Reserve, South West Nature Reserve) with size and proclamation year per park, but no machine-readable register and no Government Notice references. Communal conservancies are registered by MEFT under s.24A of the Nature Conservation Ordinance; the most complete public list is NACSO's table (86 conservancies, matching MEFT's stated 86) plus NACSO's compilation of gazette numbers. A further conservancy (Ekango Lyomongwa) was gazetted in September 2025. Community forests (Forest Act 2001) and inland fisheries reserves (Inland Fisheries Resources Act 2003) were enumerated directly from the Government Gazettes hosted by NACSO. The marine protected area is the Namibian Islands' Marine Protected Area (Marine Resources Act 2000). Comparison: the sources reviewed list 166 nationally designated or proposed areas; 15 are catalogued here, and 151 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 5 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.
gaps: MEFT gives proclamation years and sizes but not the Government Notice numbers for the 20 state protected areas; the specific notices (e.g. Bwabwata 2007, Dorob 2010, Tsau //Khaeb 2008, Mangetti 2008, Nkasa Rupara renaming) were not verified (NamibLII was behind a bot challenge).
'South West Nature Reserve' appears in MEFT's list but its link points to the Skeleton Coast page; its location, size and legal basis could not be verified.

MEFT's state-protected-area list does not include the Namibian Islands' Marine Protected Area, Cape Cross is listed as a 'Seal Reserve', and Gross-Barmen / Hardap / Von Bach / Naute are recreation-oriented game parks or resorts; categories here follow MEFT labels.
Conservancy registrations after 2018 other than Ekango Lyomongwa (GN 248 of 2025) could not be checked systematically; the NACSO/MEFT count of 86 may be out of date.

NACSO says '43 registered and emerging' community forests, but 47 gazetted declarations (2006-2023) were found in the gazettes NACSO hosts; the gazette list is used here and community forests declared outside these gazettes may be missing.
GN 297 of 2016 declares the whole Zambezi/Chobe River system a seasonal fisheries reserve (1 December to 28 February each year); it is a seasonal closure and is not recorded as an area.

No official coordinates were used; points depend on Wikidata matches. Wikidata was heavily rate-limited (HTTP 429) during this run, so only a keyword search (haswbstatement:P17) was possible; most conservancies, community forests and fisheries reserves appear to have no Wikidata item and have null QIDs.
Not enumerated: freehold conservancies — Voluntary associations of commercial farmers; not declared under the Nature Conservation Ordinance's protected-area provisions and no official list found.
Not enumerated: tourism and hunting concessions — Use rights granted by MEFT inside/outside parks, not protected-area designations.
Not enumerated: private game parks / private nature reserves (s.22 of the Ordinance) — No official list found.
Not enumerated: state forest reserves other than Zambezi — Only the 2023 Zambezi State Forest Reserve declaration was found; no consolidated list of state forest reserves was located.
151 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: No consolidated official list or protected-area authority website was found. The inventory is reconstructed from the founding legal texts in the Diário da República (via FAOLEX): Laws 6/2006 and 7/2006 creating the two terrestrial natural parks, and Decree-Laws 02/2026 (national MPA network framework) and 03/2026 (first two MPAs of São Tomé). The six MPAs planned around Príncipe are to be classified by a separate Príncipe regional instrument, which was not found. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 4 nationally designated or proposed areas; 2 are catalogued here, and 2 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 1 Ramsar site for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.

officialCounts.category: marine protected areas of São Tomé island (created)
marine protected areas planned (6 Príncipe + 2 São Tomé) — NGO figure

gaps: Neither park law states a total area, so areaKm2 is null for both natural parks; no official area figure was found.
No official coordinates were found. The park laws describe boundaries by named landmarks and maps, and the MPA zoning maps are annexes (images) in the decree-law.

The legal status of the six planned Príncipe MPAs could not be confirmed. NGO sources (PGA 2025, Fauna & Flora 2025) report draft decree-laws approved by the Council of Ministers in April 2025, but only the São Tomé decree (03/2026) was found in FAOLEX.
Decree-Laws 02/2026 and 03/2026 enter into force 90 days after publication (about late May 2026); no later implementing acts (management plans) were checked.
The NGO factsheet says the whole country was designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve on 27 September 2025. This is left to the coordinator's UNESCO check and not used here.
Ramsar (e.g. Ilhéus Tinhosas, mentioned in the 6th national report as a Ramsar site since 2006) and biosphere designations are not recorded as separate areas, per the brief.
Wikidata QIDs for the two natural parks were checked with Special:EntityData. No Wikidata items were found for the two 2026 MPAs.

Not enumerated: marine protected areas of the Autonomous Region of Príncipe (planned) (about 6) — Decree-Law 02/2026 leaves the classification of Príncipe MPAs to a separate instrument ('diploma próprio'). No published Príncipe instrument was found, and the site names appear only on an NGO map image, so they are not listed individually.
2 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: No single consolidated official list. Inventories are split by managing authority: TANAPA (national parks; 21 park sections on its website, Kigosi National Park was revoked by GN 616 of 2023), TAWA (an official table of game reserves, game controlled areas and wildlife management areas with area, region and gazettement GN), NCAA (Ngorongoro Conservation Area), the Marine Parks and Reserves Unit (3 marine parks + 15 marine reserves, Tanzania mainland), and TFS (465 forest reserves incl. 25 nature forest reserves and 18 bee reserves; no public list). Zanzibar's protected areas are managed separately by the Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar; no official Zanzibar list could be fetched. Legal instruments (GNs) are indexed on TanzLII. The TAWA table is the most complete official list; the TANAPA list comes from the site's park sections, not from a stated list. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 124 nationally designated or proposed areas; 31 are catalogued here, and 93 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 4 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.
gaps: TANAPA's website lists 21 national parks but does not state a total count, establishment instruments or areas for most parks; the original declaration GNs for the 2019 parks (Burigi-Chato, Ibanda-Kyerwa, Rumanyika-Karagwe, Ugalla-River, Nyerere) were not found.

Kigosi National Park (2019) is excluded: GN 616 of 2023 ('Tamko la Kufuta Hifadhi ya Taifa Kigosi la Mwaka 2023') revoked it per TanzLII; a 2025 High Court judgment indexed on TanzLII describes the area as now 'Hifadhi ya Msitu ya Taifa Kigosi' (national forest reserve), which could not be confirmed from TFS.

TanzLII document pages (National Parks Act Cap 282 consolidated 2025 with its Second Schedule; individual GNs) are behind a Cloudflare challenge; only titles, GN numbers and dates from the TanzLII search API were used.

TAWA's table has 25 game reserve rows (two rows combine two reserves: Ikorongo & Grumeti; Lukwati & Piti), versus 28 game reserves in the 2014 CBD report; some reserves were upgraded to national parks since 2019 (e.g. Burigi, Biharamulo, Kimisi, Ibanda, Rumanyika, Kigosi, Ugalla parts). TAWA areas are rounded figures for many reserves.
TAWA's table lists 25 game controlled areas and 21 WMAs, versus 42 GCAs and 38 WMAs (33 established) in the 2014 CBD report; differences could not be reconciled.

Marine reserve names are given by MPRU only as island names; individual gazettement years are known only for the four DMRS islands gazetted in June 1975. Mnazi Bay-Ruvuma Estuary Marine Park's gazettement could not be read from the GMP PDF.

Zanzibar: Jozani-Chwaka Bay National Park, Changuu-Bawe and other Zanzibar conservation areas could not be verified from official sources; the three Zanzibar marine areas are recorded only from the 2014 CBD report.

Ramsar sites (Malagarasi-Muyovozi, Kilombero Valley Floodplain, Lake Natron) and the Kilwa/Songo Mnara cultural heritage site appear in the TAWA table but are not recorded as separate areas per the brief.
No official coordinates were found for any area.

Wikidata QIDs were matched (search + entity check of label, P17 country and P31 type) only for national parks and selected major reserves; the Wikidata API was heavily rate-limited (HTTP 429) during this run, so other areas were not attempted or the lookup failed. A null QID does not mean no item exists.

Not enumerated: forest reserves (TFS national forest reserves, incl. remaining nature forest reserves) (about 465) — No official list published on the TFS website; only 8 destination pages found. Local authority forest reserves and village land forest reserves are additional.

Not enumerated: national bee reserves (about 18) — TFS states 18 bee reserves but publishes no list; several were declared by GN in 2024 (e.g. Malinga GN 526, Aghondi GN 530, Kwenyunga-Magiri GN 550, Shinji GN 551 of 2024 per TanzLII). Bee reserves are forest/beekeeping reserves rather than wildlife conservation areas.

Not enumerated: Zanzibar terrestrial protected areas (e.g. Jozani-Chwaka Bay National Park, forest reserves) — No Zanzibar Government source could be fetched (sites unreachable or blocked); only third-party sources were found, so none are recorded.

Not enumerated: wildlife corridors and other recent wildlife declarations — Only the Nyerere-Udzungwa corridor (GN 226 of 2025) was found; a systematic search of TanzLII for all corridor orders was not possible because full-text pages are blocked to automated fetch.
93 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

inventory.summary: Uganda Wildlife Authority manages the wildlife conservation areas and states their counts (10 national parks, 12 wildlife reserves, 5 community wildlife management areas, 13 wildlife sanctuaries) but its website names only the national parks and 11 wildlife reserves. The legal declarations are statutory instruments under the Uganda Wildlife Act (most from 2003, SI 41–64 of 2003), indexed on ULII. The National Forestry Authority manages 506 central forest reserves (no list published on its website); local forest reserves are managed by district governments. Comparison: the sources reviewed list 31 nationally designated or proposed areas; 22 are catalogued here (1 as an extra designation on an already catalogued area), and 9 are verified but not yet mapped because no openly licensed location was found. The catalogue also holds 12 Ramsar sites for this country. Coverage has not been verified as exhaustive.
gaps: ULII document pages are behind a Cloudflare challenge; only instrument titles, numbers and dates from the ULII search API were used. SI 60 of 2003 (gap in the series 41–64) could not be identified.

No 2003-era declaration instruments were found for Kidepo Valley, Murchison Falls, Rwenzori Mountains and Semuliki national parks or for Katonga, Karuma and Kigezi wildlife reserves; these may have been declared under earlier legislation (e.g. National Parks Act; National Parks (Declaration) (Amendment) Order, SI 76 of 1993).

UWA page areas are headline figures; the Kibale figure (321 km², identical to Bwindi) appears erroneous and was omitted; Ajai, Karuma and Kigezi pages give inconsistent km²/ha pairs (km² value recorded).
Whether East Madi is UWA's 12th wildlife reserve is inferred, not confirmed.
Ramsar sites and World Heritage sites (Bwindi, Rwenzori) are noted only where they coincide with a park.
No official coordinates were found for any area.

Wikidata QIDs were matched (search + entity check of label, P17 country and P31 type) only for national parks and selected major reserves; the Wikidata API was heavily rate-limited (HTTP 429) during this run, so other areas were not attempted or the lookup failed. A null QID does not mean no item exists.

Not enumerated: central forest reserves (about 506) — NFA states 506 CFRs (1,265,741 ha) but its CFR catalogue page does not list them; the declaring orders (Forest (Declaration of Central Forest Reserves) Orders) are on ULII but full text is blocked to automated fetch.
Not enumerated: local forest reserves — Managed by District Local Governments (NFA catalogue page); no list found.

Not enumerated: wildlife sanctuaries not found in legal records (about 8) — UWA states 13 sanctuaries; only 5 declaration instruments (2003) were found on ULII and UWA's sanctuary page shows only Ziwa Rhino Sanctuary (privately run; legal status not verified).
Not enumerated: community wildlife areas not found in legal records (about 1) — UWA states 5; only 4 declaration instruments (2003) were found on ULII.
9 verified areas not mapped (no openly licensed coordinates); listed in docs/inventory/uncatalogued-areas.csv.
WDPA/Protected Planet, the most complete global compilation, is not used because its licence does not allow redistribution here, so the catalogue cannot be compared with it.

location.description: Atlantic archipelago off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, described by UNESCO as the only active deltaic archipelago on the African Atlantic coast.

geometry.caveat: The outline is the Bolama administrative region (geoBoundaries ADM1, from OpenStreetMap), which contains the archipelago. It is not the boundary of the Biosphere Reserve, the Ramsar site or the World Heritage property.

overview.text: The Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 under natural criteria (ix) and (x).
The Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve was designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1996.
The archipelago was designated a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2014 (site 'Archipel Bolama-Bijagós').
Three marine protected areas — João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park, Orango Islands National Park and the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area — were created in 2000 and 2005.
UNESCO identifies the archipelago as the second most important foraging area in Africa for migratory waterbirds of the East Atlantic Flyway, and as a sanctuary for a diversity of sharks and rays.
UNESCO attributes the property's exceptional state of conservation mainly to how the area is organised and to traditional resource management by local communities.
Sacred islands governed by customary rules act as refuges for biodiversity.
Overall management of the World Heritage property is coordinated by the Institute for Biodiversity and Protected Areas (IBAP).

BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project aims to establish a community marine protected area on the islands of Unhocomo and Unhocomozinho, recognised as sanctuaries for juvenile sea turtles (proposal, not yet designated).
Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025 as a natural property (“Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô”).

livelihoods.text: Agriculture, forest use, animal husbandry, fishing, shell gathering and ecological tourism are the main activities of island communities.
The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Shellfish are the principal source of animal protein for island communities.
Tourism in the archipelago has developed over recent decades but remains limited.

ecosystems.text: The site features mangroves, mudflats and intertidal zones vital for marine life.
Intertidal mud and sand flats are among the Ramsar wetland types recorded for the archipelago.
Shallow marine waters are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the archipelago.
Estuarine waters are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the archipelago.
Key intertidal areas include extensive, highly productive seagrass beds.
On land, the islands have palm groves, littoral woodland savannas and semi-dry forests.

verification.note: Designations, key ecological facts and livelihoods checked against UNESCO, Ramsar, IBAP and BioGuinea sources. The map outline is an administrative proxy, not a designated-site boundary.

territories.name: Orango Islands National Park
territories.localName: Parque Nacional das Ilhas de Orango

location.description: In the extreme south-west of the Bijagós Archipelago.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata. The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: Created in 2000, Orango National Park is a core area of the Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve and is classified as IUCN Category II.
The archipelago, notably Orango, hosts hippopotamuses that live in seawater on an almost permanent basis — according to UNESCO, the only place in the world where the species does so.
Five of the world's seven sea turtle species frequent the park's beaches.
The park is also home to several monkey species, African manatees and several reptile species.
The park includes 33 villages with an estimated 3,369 inhabitants, mainly of the Bijagó ethnic group.
Listed as “Parque Nacional” by República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

livelihoods.text: Activities in the park include farming (rice, oil palm and cashew), shellfish gathering, fishing and crafts.
A community guest house in the village of Anôr serves as a base for visitors to this part of Orango Island.

ecosystems.text: The park's beaches are used by five sea turtle species.
The park's hippos live in the sea, unlike freshwater populations elsewhere.

verification.note: Creation year, classification, key species and livelihoods verified. Location is a representative point only, and habitat detail specific to the park is limited in this dataset. National designation from República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

legalStatus.text: Created by Decreto n.º 11/2000 (BO n.º 49, 4 December 2000).

territories.name: João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park
territories.localName: Parque Nacional Marinho João Vieira e Poilão

location.description: Group of islands within the Bijagós Archipelago, including Poilão Island.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata. The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: Created in August 2000 for complete protection as an integral reserve, and classified as IUCN Category II.
Poilão Island is a globally important nesting site for sea turtles.
The park is described as the second most important green turtle (Chelonia mydas) nesting site in the South Atlantic.

Listed as “Parque Nacional Marinho” by República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

ecosystems.text: Key intertidal areas include extensive and highly productive seagrass beds.
Mudflats are among the park's key intertidal habitats.
Mangroves are among the park's key intertidal habitats.
A highly dynamic coastline radically changes beach profiles across the park's islands, which host major turtle nesting.
The park includes shallow areas up to the 10-metre isobath.

verification.note: Creation date, protection status, habitats and turtle significance verified. Location is a representative point only. No source describing local livelihoods in the park was reviewed. National designation from República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

legalStatus.text: Created by Decreto n.º 6-A/2000 of 23 August 2000 (BO n.º 34, 2.º Suplemento).

location.description: Northern part of the Bijagós Archipelago; its main islands are Formosa, Nago and Chediã.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata. The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: Created in 2005 by Indigenous Bijagós communities to strengthen social, cultural and environmental resilience.
The area is managed directly by local communities with support from IBAP and the Guinean NGO Tiniguena.
It covers a total area of 545 km² and is classified as IUCN Category VI.
Its management council received the Equator Prize in 2019.

Listed as “Área Marinha Protegida Comunitária” by República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

livelihoods.text: The protected area aims to help communities manage their marine resources more sustainably and to secure their access to prime fishing grounds.

verification.note: Governance, creation and size verified. No source reviewed so far describes the area's specific habitats, so none are listed. Location is a representative point only. National designation from República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

location.description: Administrative region in north-western Guinea-Bissau on the border with Senegal, crossed by the Cacheu River on its way to the Atlantic.

geometry.caveat: The outline is the Cacheu administrative region (geoBoundaries ADM1, from OpenStreetMap). The Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park lies within it but its boundary is not shown.

overview.text: The Rio Cacheu is not a river in the strict sense but a ria, where the sea reaches more than 150 km inland.
The region contains the Cacheu River mangroves, considered the largest continuous block of mangroves in West Africa.

livelihoods.text: Communities in and around the Cacheu park practise a sophisticated form of rice farming on mangrove soils, a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups (notably Felupe and Baiote).

ecosystems.text: The lower Cacheu River is a tidal ria with estuarine waters.
Mangroves of the lower Cacheu River form the core of the Ramsar-listed Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park.

verification.note: Boundary and location are sourced. Most ecological and socio-economic information in this dataset comes from sources about the Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park and its buffer zone, and is linked to the region for that reason. Region-wide statistics are not included.

territories.name: Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park
territories.localName: Parque Natural dos Tarrafes do Rio Cacheu

location.description: North-western Guinea-Bissau, on the Atlantic coast near the border with Senegal, along the lower Cacheu River.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata, close to the Ramsar-listed coordinates (12°17'40"N 16°11'38"W). The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: Created in December 2000 by Decree-Law no. 12/2000 and managed by IBAP.
Wetland of International Importance (Ramsar site no. 2229) since 22 May 2015, with a listed area of 88,615 ha.
Its mangroves are considered the largest continuous mangrove block in West Africa; six mangrove species have been recorded.
The park's aims are to protect mangroves as the basis for fish reproduction, to conserve biodiversity and to improve living conditions of residents.
The mangroves provide food and refuge for protected or rare species such as the hippopotamus and the West African manatee, and serve as spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Each village in the site keeps one or more sacred forests, which act as reservoirs of biodiversity.
Listed as “Parque Natural” by República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

livelihoods.text: Besides rice fields, the mangrove provides fish, timber, honey, salt and traditional medicine.
Mangrove rice farming here is a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups and is described as unique cultural heritage.

ecosystems.text: Intertidal mangrove forest is the park's dominant wetland type.
Estuarine waters are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the site.
Intertidal mud, sand or salt flats are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the site.
Seagrass beds occur in the park and its buffer zone.
Beyond the mangroves, the landscape is a mosaic of forests, palm groves and savanna, with dryland forests in the buffer zone.

verification.note: Designations, management, ecosystems and pressures verified against Ramsar, IBAP and NGO sources. Sources disagree on the exact creation day (1 or 4 December 2000) and on the mangrove share of the park, so those details are omitted. BioGuinea lists it as a national park, while IBAP, Ramsar and Wetlands International call it a natural park; the official name is kept here. Location is a representative point only. National designation from República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

legalStatus.text: Created by Decreto n.º 12/2000 (BO n.º 49, 4 December 2000).

location.description: Southern Guinea-Bissau, in the Tombali administrative region.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata. The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: According to the BioGuinea Foundation, the park was established in 2008 and covers 1,068 km². Other public records differ (see next fact), so the creation date and area are unconfirmed.
Wikidata records different values: inception in 1980 and in October 2007, and areas of 680 km² and 1,057.67 km².
Species listed by the BioGuinea Foundation include chimpanzees, Temminck's red colobus, baboons, roan antelope, waterbuck and buffalo.
The BioGuinea Foundation runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.
Wetlands International reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.
Listed as “Parque Nacional” by República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

ecosystems.text: The BioGuinea Foundation describes the park as holding the last areas of dense sub-humid forest in the country.
Mangroves in the park are among those whose conservation Wetlands International reports supporting.

verification.note: Location and region from Wikidata. Creation year and area are as reported by BioGuinea; Wikidata lists other dates (1980, 2007) and areas (680 and 1,057.67 km²), so treat them as unconfirmed. BioGuinea's description of the park's orientation conflicts with the map and was not used. No potential activity is proposed, because no reviewed source links a documented need here to a specific activity. National designation from República da Guiné-Bissau (scan hosted by IBAP); Instituto da Biodiversidade e das Áreas Protegidas (IBAP), Guiné-Bissau; Government of Guinea-Bissau / CBD Secretariat.

legalStatus.text: Created by Decreto n.º 14/2011 (BO n.º 8, Suplemento, 22 February 2011).
